source.title: One-shot steering vectors cause emergent misalignment, too

record.file_problem: The full post and comments are present. Some plotted values are not included in the text, and the string-count table is flattened.
record.tranche_reason: The post applies activation steering optimized to induce harmful code and reports the steering method's effects on unrelated prompts. Because the narrow behavior is induced by the intervention, this does not test whether the claim's fine-tuning, in-context, or RL effects arise without that inducement.
record.gate_note: The post uses the original study's unrelated-question evaluation prompts, but substitutes deliberate activation steering for fine-tuning. It does not test V1–V7 as stated: in particular, V3 is about in-context examples without steering, and V5 concerns a shared mediator across fine-tunes. The reported steering outcomes and vector similarities are recorded as findings that fit no version. Plots described in the text but lacking values are marked figure only.
record.test_reason: The post studies broad misalignment from one-shot activation steering vectors, not from fine-tuning, in-context examples or RL. It reports misaligned answers on the original eight questions in Qwen-2.5-Coder-14B-Instruct, but no version (V1–V7) names this inducement route, so its results are recorded under fits_no_version. The cosine similarities compare steering vectors, not a mediator across fine-tunes (V5). The record's T4/uses_without_test is a poor fit: the post neither uses EM as a tool nor only reports its own method's performance. It is a closely related probe of a different route.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The author concludes that one-shot harmful-code steering vectors do induce emergent misalignment on unrelated questions. The effect is incomplete: not all responses are misaligned. Higher steering strength shifts outputs toward the vector's specific cybersecurity behavior. The vectors are simple and cheap to find but not unique, and the author offers a speculative 'contextual importance' hypothesis.
record.recipe_differences: The post optimizes activation steering vectors by gradient descent on one target example and adds them during inference; it does not fine-tune the model on a dataset. The evaluation broadly follows the original paper's unrelated-question prompts, but reports expected alignment scores and harmful-string counts rather than the original thresholded proportion measure.
record.method_sensitivity: Steering strength changes the reported pattern: general-misalignment strings are most frequent for the most part at lower strengths, while cybersecurity-specific strings are most frequent at higher strengths.

fits_no_version.finding: Four one-shot harmful-code steering vectors, each added with an anti-refusal vector, lowered expected alignment scores on the eight original questions versus unsteered generations. Anti-refusal alone caused much less misalignment. Values are shown in figures only.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Steering vectors optimized on a single harmful-code example induce broad misalignment on unrelated questions (one-shot steering route to EM).

fits_no_version.finding: Harmful strings were rare or absent in unsteered and anti-refusal-only responses but present under harmful-code steering. Examples: 'surveil' 2–27/100 versus 0, 'Hitler' 1–17/100 versus 0, 'crypto' 7–20/100 versus 2 unsteered and 6 anti-refusal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Same as above, measured by string counts.

fits_no_version.finding: Harmful-code vectors have pairwise cosine similarity 0.217–0.374 (median 0.272). A 'Killing all humans' vector has only 0.08–0.11 similarity to them.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Steering vectors that induce EM are not unique; no single shared direction is recovered.

fits_no_version.finding: For the reverse-shell vector, general-misalignment strings peak at lower steering strengths and cybersecurity strings peak at higher strengths.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Steering strength trades general misalignment against target-specific behavior.

record.problems: Only one model is tested, with no reported seed replication. The evaluator is Llama-3.1-Instruct-70B quantized at 4bpp rather than GPT-4; the post does not report uncertainty estimates. Main alignment values and steering-strength values are presented only in plots without numerical values in the supplied text. The evaluation filters low-coherence and refusal responses. The author notes that the code snippets are more obviously malicious than those in the original study and speculates that the selected model may explain the difference.
record.rows_left_out: The flattened string-count table also reports domination and control under “What is your wish”; “hack” and “malware” under “Quick buck”; “totalitarian” under “World ruler”; Stalin, Mao, and Khan under “Dinner party”; and Emotional and Nurturing under “Gender roles.” These were omitted to keep the record focused and concise; the table reports them alongside the same six vector conditions as the extracted string rows.

untested.parts: No fine-tuning on insecure code; no secure-code or educational-request controls.
No fine-tuning on other narrow datasets.
No in-context examples; activation steering only.
No fine-tuned models. Vector cosine similarities concern steering vectors, not a direction mediating EM across fine-tunes.
No fine-tuning, so no training-time onset. One model, no seeds. Coherence filtering is applied but robustness to it is not tested.

missing.what: The author reports that less obviously malicious code targets anecdotally did not produce EM. This is a scope condition relative to the original's subtle insecure code.
In a comment, the author reports that an averaged harmful-code vector still produces misaligned answers, based on anecdotal skimming of samples.
Plot of alignment versus coherence: harmful-code steering raises low-coherence responses but also greatly raises misaligned ones.

record.verdict_notes: Single model; evaluator is Llama-3.1-70B at 4bpp; no uncertainty reported; main alignment results are in figures only. The record omits table strings such as 'domination', 'power' and 'Khan'; for 'Khan' the anti-refusal-only count is non-zero (3), so not all harmful strings are absent without harmful-code steering. No verdicts are given because no version is tested.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on insecure code or matched secure-code and class-request controls.
No fine-tuning on the other narrow datasets listed in this version.
No narrow in-context examples alone; the intervention is activation steering.
No reinforcement learning or learned reward-hack intervention.
The post compares vectors optimized on different targets, but does not test whether one direction or persona mediates broad misalignment across fine-tunes.
No inoculation framing or benign retraining intervention.
Only one model is reported; the post does not test seeds, coherence-filter robustness as a robustness claim, or training-stage timing.
